pages.name: Coil up, capacitor down
pages.text: A resistor, a coil and a capacitor each hold back an alternating current, and each one's opposition is counted in ohms. On the complex plane the resistor's lies along the real axis, the coil's points straight up and the capacitor's points straight down.

pages.name: A 10 Ω capacitor
pages.task: A capacitor holds back the current by 10 Ω. Which complex number is its opposition?
pages.why: A capacitor's opposition is a quarter turn clockwise from the real axis, straight down. So its 10 Ω becomes `−j10`. The size, 10 Ω, is its reactance; the −j comes from it being a capacitor.

pages.name: Why straight up
pages.text: Why straight up? A coil's voltage follows how fast its current changes. The current changes fastest as it crosses zero, and stops changing for an instant at its peak.
pages.alt: A current arrow and a coil voltage arrow turning in a circle, and the waves their heights trace out over time. The current wave. The coil voltage wave, a quarter cycle ahead. A bracket along the time axis marks a quarter cycle between the voltage's peak and the current's.

pages.name: Current crossing zero
pages.task: The current through a coil is crossing zero on its way up, at the dashed line. What is the coil's voltage doing then?
pages.why: A coil's voltage follows how fast its current changes. Crossing zero on its way up, the current is rising at its fastest, so the coil's voltage is at its peak. A quarter cycle later the current peaks and stops changing for an instant, and the voltage is zero.

pages.name: The builder
pages.text: The sizes depend on the frequency f. A wave twice as steep doubles a coil's voltage for the same current, and drives twice the current through a capacitor for the same voltage. So a coil's reactance is `X_L = 2πfL` and a capacitor's is `X_C = 1 ÷ (2πfC)`, with L in henries and C in farads.

pages.name: At 100 Hz
pages.task: Double the frequency to 100 Hz, with the same 19.1 mH coil and 318 µF capacitor. What are the two reactances now?
pages.why: `X_L = 2πfL` has f on top, so doubling f doubles 6.0 Ω to 12.0 Ω. `X_C = 1 ÷ (2πfC)` has f underneath, so doubling f halves 10.0 Ω to 5.0 Ω. Now the coil wins, and Z swings above the real axis.

pages.name: Length and angle
pages.text: An 8 Ω resistor with that 6 Ω coil gives `Z = 8 + j6`. The coil's 6 Ω stands at a quarter turn to the 8, so the sizes combine by Pythagoras, not by adding.

pages.name: 8 Ω with a 6 Ω coil
pages.task: An 8 Ω resistor is in series with a 6 Ω coil. How many ohms is Z, its length?
pages.why: The coil's 6 Ω points straight up from the tip of the resistor's 8 Ω, so Z is the long side of a right-angled triangle: `√(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10` Ω, at `tan⁻¹(6 ÷ 8) = 36.87°`.

pages.name: Coil against capacitor
pages.text: Raise the frequency and the coil's arrow grows while the capacitor's shrinks. Near 65 Hz they all but cancel, and Z comes within 0.1 Ω of the 8 Ω resistor alone. Past that the coil wins, and Z points up.

pages.name: All three in series
pages.task: An 8 Ω resistor, a 6 Ω coil and a 10 Ω capacitor are in series. What is Z?
pages.why: Give each part its direction: the resistor 8, the coil +j6, the capacitor −j10. In series they add tip to tail, `Z = 8 + j(6 − 10) = 8 − j4`. The capacitor's arrow is longer, so Z dips below the real axis.

pages.text: Going the other way, a Z given as a length and an angle splits back into its parts. The real part is the resistance, and the j part is the reactance.

pages.name: 5∠−53.13° in parts
pages.task: An impedance is `Z = 5∠−53.13°`. What is it in parts?
pages.why: `R = 5 cos(−53.13°) = 3` and `X = 5 sin(−53.13°) = −4`. So `Z = 3 − j4`: 3 Ω of resistance, and the capacitor wins by 4 Ω, so Z points down.

pages.name: At double the frequency
pages.task: A 6 Ω resistor is in series with a coil of 4 Ω at 50 Hz. What is Z at 100 Hz, as a length and an angle?
pages.why: `X_L = 2πfL` grows in step with f, so doubling f doubles the coil's 4 Ω to 8 Ω. Then `Z = 6 + j8`, with length `√(36 + 64) = 10` and angle `tan⁻¹(8 ÷ 6) = 53.13°`. So `Z = 10∠53.13°`.
